c.tagline: Golden-sandstone university city where students fill the tapas bars beneath Spain's grandest Plaza Mayor.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered; Cabify operates in the city but there is no Uber. Ranks sit at Plaza Mayor, the train station and the bus station.

emergency.note: 112 is the Europe-wide emergency number connecting to police, ambulance and fire, free from any phone.

hood_landmark.Barrio del Oeste: Barrio del Oeste street art, Salamanca

avoid.reason: Minor pickpocketing around the Plaza Mayor in peak tourist periods, and student nightlife streets get rowdy in the small hours.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed heart of the city around Plaza Mayor, the University of Salamanca, the two cathedrals and the Casa de las Conchas; almost entirely pedestrian and best for first-timers who want every sight on their doorstep.
A creative, working-class district just west of the centre famous for its open-air street-art murals, indie cafes and studios; suits younger travellers after a bohemian, less touristy vibe.
An elegant, quiet residential quarter of golden-sandstone mansions bordering the old town near the Parque de los Jesuitas; calm and central, good for couples and families.
The relaxed area across the Roman bridge on the south bank of the River Tormes, with river walks and views back to the illuminated cathedrals; quieter and cheaper than the core.
lodging: Hotel Ele Puente Romano de Salamanca

water.note: Tap water is safe and good quality.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6:30am to 11pm, with a limited búho night-bus service on weekends.
transit.note: Salamanca has no metro or tram; the compact UNESCO old town is almost entirely walkable and a network of urban buses covers the outskirts.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash (about €1.15 single) or tap a rechargeable Bono Bus card for cheaper fares; contactless bank-card payment is being rolled out on buses.

air: Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas (MAD) — main long-haul gateway, ~2.5h by coach
bus: Salamanca bus station — Avanza and ALSA coaches
train: Salamanca railway station — high-speed Alvia to Madrid (~1.5h)

transit.m: Most travellers fly into Madrid-Barajas (MAD) and take the Avanza coach (~2.5h) or Alvia train (~1.5h) on to Salamanca
Taxi from Salamanca Airport to the city centre (~20 min)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Hornazo
food.desc: Salamanca's dense savoury pie - lard pastry packed with pork loin, chorizo, cured ham and hard-boiled egg, eaten cold in slabs.

places.name: Mercado Central de Abastos
places.note: Charcuterie and bakery stalls sell hornazo by weight; the local way to buy it for a picnic.

places.name: Casa Paca
places.note: Old-guard Salamanca restaurant, a safe bet for the province's traditional dishes.

places.name: Meson Las Conchas
places.note: Busy tapas house near the Casa de las Conchas serving hornazo, farinato and local cured meats.

food.name: Farinato
food.desc: The poor man's chorizo - pork fat, flour, paprika and aniseed, fried in slices and served with fried eggs on top.

places.name: Meson Las Conchas
places.note: Named repeatedly for its farinato con huevos, one of the most Salamancan plates in the city.

places.name: Bar Bambu
places.note: Cult tapas bar off Plaza Mayor; free tapa with every drink and a strong local repertoire.

places.name: Mercado Central de Abastos
places.note: Butchers sell farinato and local chorizo to cook at home or hand to a nearby bar kitchen.

food.name: Jamon iberico de Guijuelo
food.desc: Acorn-fed Iberian ham cured in the cold mountain air of Guijuelo, an hour south - sliced paper thin and eaten with nothing else.

places.name: Mercado Central de Abastos
places.note: Specialist ham stalls slice Guijuelo bellota to order at far below restaurant prices.

places.name: Casa Paca
places.note: Traditional dining room with a good iberico board to open a Castilian meal.

places.name: El Meson de Gonzalo
places.note: Well-regarded kitchen beside Plaza Mayor known for iberico products and updated classics.

food.name: Chanfaina salmantina
food.desc: Hearty shepherd's rice cooked with lamb offal, blood sausage and paprika - rustic, rich and the definitive winter dish here.

places.name: Casa Paca
places.note: One of the few central restaurants that keeps chanfaina on the traditional menu.

places.name: El Meson de Gonzalo
places.note: Provincial recipes handled with care, including offal dishes locals actually order.

places.name: Meson Las Conchas
places.note: Casual place to try chanfaina and other Salamanca specialities as a raciones plate.

food.name: Tostones and chuleton de Morucha
food.desc: Thick-cut roast suckling pig and enormous grilled steaks from the local Morucha cattle, salted and seared over embers.

places.name: El Meson de Gonzalo
places.note: Its charcoal-grilled Morucha steak is one of the best-known plates in the city.

places.name: Casa Paca
places.note: Castilian roast meats served in a wood-panelled dining room since the mid 20th century.

places.name: La Cocina de Tono
places.note: Long-praised tapas and dining room mixing classic Salamanca meat with modern plates.

food.name: Free tapas crawl
food.desc: Order a drink in Salamanca and a tapa arrives free - pinchos of tortilla, patatas bravas, morcilla or jeta, bar after bar.

places.name: Bar Bambu
places.note: The classic first stop; standing room only, generous free tapas with every cana.

places.name: Calle Van Dyck bars
places.note: Student tapas street north of the centre where the plates are biggest and prices lowest.

places.name: Tapas 3.0
places.note: Creative small plates from a kitchen that has drawn national attention for its modern tapas.

food.name: Castilian red wine
food.desc: Tempranillo from Ribera del Duero and Toro plus the local Sierra de Salamanca Rufete - poured by the glass in every bar.

places.name: La Cocina de Tono
places.note: Serious wine list of Castilla y Leon bottles matched to the tapas.

places.name: Casa Paca
places.note: Deep cellar of Ribera and Toro reds to go with the roast meats.

places.name: Mercado Central de Abastos
places.note: Market wine bars pour regional glasses alongside ham and cheese plates at midday.

food.name: Vermut de grifo
food.desc: House vermouth on tap with ice, orange and an olive - the Spanish pre-lunch ritual, taken on a Plaza Mayor terrace.

places.name: Cafe Novelty
places.note: Salamanca's oldest cafe, open since 1905, with terrace tables under the arcades.

places.name: Bar Bambu
places.note: Vermouth and a free tapa is the standard Sunday noon order here.

places.name: Meson Las Conchas
places.note: Terrace vermouth with cured meats a few steps from the university quarter.

landmarks: Plaza Mayor
Spain's most beautiful baroque square, a golden-sandstone arcade by the Churriguera brothers that glows unforgettably when the evening lights come on.
Universidad de Salamanca (University Facade)
The Plateresque facade of Spain's oldest university, founded in 1218, where visitors squint to find the lucky frog perched on a carved skull.
Catedral Nueva y Catedral Vieja (New and Old Cathedrals)
Two joined cathedrals spanning Romanesque to Gothic-baroque, with a famous carved astronaut on the portal and tower walkways along the Ieronimus route.
Casa de las Conchas
A late-Gothic palace armoured with more than 300 carved scallop shells, emblem of the Order of Santiago, now a public library with a lovely courtyard.
La Clerecía (Pontifical University)
A towering baroque Jesuit college whose Scala Coeli tower climb rewards visitors with the finest rooftop panorama over Salamanca's golden skyline.
Convento de San Esteban
A magnificent Dominican monastery with a triumphal-arch Plateresque facade, where Columbus reputedly defended his westward voyage before university scholars.
Casa Lis (Museo Art Nouveau y Art Déco)
A jewel-box iron-and-stained-glass mansion above the old walls, filled with Lalique glass, porcelain dolls and the glamour of the Belle Époque.
Puente Romano (Roman Bridge)
A 26-arch Roman bridge carrying the Silver Way across the Tormes since the first century, offering the classic postcard view of the cathedrals.
Convento de las Dueñas
A Dominican convent whose irregular Renaissance cloister hides wildly imaginative carved capitals, and whose nuns still sell celebrated almond sweets.
Huerto de Calixto y Melibea
A romantic walled garden by the old city ramparts, the legendary setting of La Celestina, with dreamy views towards cathedral and river.

train.note: No international trains, though Salamanca sits on the historic line toward the Portuguese border at Fuentes de Oñoro - the through Madrid-Lisbon service that once used it was withdrawn and has not returned. Alvia trains reach Madrid Chamartín in about 1h40 and there are regional services to Valladolid and Ávila. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: The bus station is northwest of the old town, about 15 minutes' walk from the Plaza Mayor. ALSA runs the cross-border services into northern Portugal as well as frequent domestic buses to Madrid (about 2h30), Valladolid and Zamora. Bring your passport or EU ID card for the Portuguese routes.

ferry.note: Salamanca is inland on the Tormes, which is not navigable, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Ávila
half.blurb: A walled medieval city about an hour and 15 minutes away has one of Europe's best-preserved sets of medieval fortifications, still fully encircling the old town.

half.name: Ciudad Rodrigo
half.blurb: A walled border town about an hour away has a 12th-century cathedral and ramparts overlooking the Águeda River.

half.name: La Alberca
half.blurb: A mountain village about an hour and 15 minutes away preserves half-timbered stone houses and cobbled streets in the Sierra de Francia.

half.name: Toro
half.blurb: A wine town about an hour away has a Romanesque collegiate church and cellars producing Toro-region red wines.

full.name: Segovia
full.blurb: A city about two hours away has a Roman aqueduct still standing after nearly two thousand years and a fairy-tale Alcázar castle.
